title: Too many hours in meetings each week: how product managers cut them on Mac
metaTitle: Too many hours in meetings each week: fixes for product managers
description: Too many hours in meetings each week is common for product managers. Here is what it costs, why it happens, and fixes you can start today on Mac.
targetKeyword: too many hours in meetings each week
secondaryKeywords: how many hours in meetings is too many
reduce meetings as a product manager
intro: If you have too many hours in meetings each week, you are in common company. Harvard Business Review reports that executives average nearly 23 hours a week in meetings. This page covers what that time costs, why calendars fill up, and fixes you can start this week without buying anything.
tldr: Too many meeting hours are usually a process problem: long defaults, recurring invites and meetings with no clear purpose.
An MIT Sloan study of 76 companies linked two meeting-free days a week to 71% higher reported productivity.
Shorten default meeting lengths, end early and replace status meetings with written updates.
Outlook for Mac can shorten every event. The setting sits in Outlook > Preferences > Calendar.
Lazur can draft decline notes, take dictated agendas and add Calendar events by voice. It does not click buttons for you.

blocks.text: Start with your own number, not the average. Open last week's calendar and add up the hours you spent in meetings. Then ask how many of those hours produced a decision, a finished document or a teammate who could move. The gap between those two answers is your excess. That gap is the part worth fixing.
How many hours in meetings is too many?

No study gives one number that fits every role. The research gives benchmarks instead. Harvard Business Review reports that executives spend nearly 23 hours a week in meetings. Microsoft's telemetry shows weekly meetings per average Teams user rose 153% since the start of the pandemic, as of its September 2022 report. A benchmark shows the trend is common. It does not tell you whether your week is healthy.

A better test is about your work. If meetings push deep work into the evening, or you cannot finish a spec during working hours, the total is too high for you. Microsoft's June 2025 report found meetings after 8 pm rose 16% year over year. Late calls often mean the calendar has run out of edges.
Run a quick audit of last week's calendar

Open last week's calendar and make a simple log. Tag each meeting with one label: decision, update or relationship. If you want a running record, paste the tags into a Google Sheets tab. Then total the minutes for each label.

items: Tag each meeting as decision, update or relationship.
Mark each meeting where you talked for less than half the time.
Flag every update that could have been a written note.
Total the minutes per tag, then compare that total with your focus time.

blocks.title: Keep the audit rough
blocks.text: Do the audit in one sitting with rough tags. Precision matters less than seeing the pattern in one view. Refine next week, once you know which recurring series to attack first.
What excess meetings cost you

The costs show up in three places: your focus, your evenings and your pay. The cost list on this page covers each one. Read every number here as a signal, not a verdict on your week. Most of the figures come from surveys, telemetry or small studies.

The best quantitative study on cutting meetings comes from MIT Sloan Management Review. It covers 76 companies with more than 1,000 employees each, in more than 50 countries. Companies that added two no-meeting days a week, and cut meetings by 40%, reported 71% higher productivity. The figures come from employee pulse surveys, so they show what people said, not what got measured.

blocks.caption: Self-reported gains from pulse surveys in MIT Sloan's study of 76 companies.

blocks.title: Do not aim for zero meetings
blocks.text: The benefits level off once meetings fall 60%, and they fade beyond that. Full elimination lowers satisfaction, productivity and engagement, according to the same article. Aim for a steady cut, not an empty calendar.
Why your calendar fills up

Take a weekly sync that started as a launch check. A few months later it covers the roadmap, bug triage and a status update nobody reads. Nobody voted to make it longer. It just kept its slot on the calendar.

Most invites trace back to one cause. Tracing it matters because the fix changes with the cause. A default needs a setting. A status meeting needs a written update. A missing spec needs a document, not a call.
Fixes you can use without buying anything

Start with your own calendar. These changes cost nothing, and you can undo them in a minute. Team rules come next, because they need agreement. Skip a company-wide meeting ban at first. It needs buy-in you may not have yet.
Shorten default meeting lengths

Google's Workspace hybrid work help suggests changing the default meeting duration in event settings from 30 minutes to 25 minutes. It also suggests ending meetings 5 to 10 minutes before the hour, so people can reset between calls. Google gives no outcome data for either change. Your admin may control these settings, so check with IT before you change them for a team.

On a Mac, Outlook can shorten every event for you. Open Outlook > Preferences > Calendar. Click Configure next to Shorten duration for all events, tick the box, choose minutes for events under one hour and for one hour or longer, then click Save. The setting applies per email account, so repeat it for each account. Press ⌘, to reach Preferences faster.
Protect one meeting-free day, then test a second

The MIT Sloan data shows a 35% reported gain with one meeting-free day and 71% with two. Pick days that fit your launch rhythm, not the days that feel easiest. Tell your team in writing, then block those days as recurring events on your calendar.

Watch for clashes. A meeting-free day can collide with customer calls, a sprint review or a partner in another region. Check those first. If Thursday is your engineering demo, use Wednesday and Friday instead. Averages hide these clashes, so your own calendar matters more.
Replace status meetings with written updates

Post the update in Slack or Notion at the time the meeting used to start. Pin it in the channel so people can find it later. Keep the live slot only for questions. A simple rule helps: if the update raises no question, it does not need a call.
A worked example for one week

Here is one way a product manager could run the week. On Monday, run the audit and tag each meeting. On Tuesday, shorten defaults in Outlook and ask the regular attendees whether a 25 minute sync works. On Wednesday, write the update that replaces one recurring meeting. On Thursday, post your proposal for a meeting-free day.

By Friday, compare the total meeting hours and the share tagged decision with Monday's log. Look for a shift, not a perfect score. If the total barely moved, pick the next largest recurring meeting and repeat the process the following week.
Using Focus and Calendar on your Mac

Apple's Focus settings can hold back interruptions while you work. Open System Settings > Focus. Allowed People and Allowed Apps let selected notifications through. Focus Filters customize how Calendar and Mail behave while a Focus is on, so those apps can behave differently during a focus block.

Apple's Focus help page is written for macOS 27, so menu names may differ on your version. Focus can sync across devices on the same Apple Account. I found no outcome data showing that Focus Filters reduce meeting load. Treat them as a tidy-up, not a cure.
Where Lazur helps, and where it does not

Lazur is a voice assistant for the Mac that lives in the notch. Hold ⌥⌘ to ask about anything on screen, and it answers out loud. Ask where a recurring invite is, and Lazur circles it. Ask how to change a setting, and Lazur guides you one click at a time, waiting for each click.

Lazur helps most with the writing and the setup. Dictate an agenda with fn, ask Lazur to draft a decline note that you then send yourself, or ask it to add a Calendar event for a focus block. It does not click buttons or operate other apps. It will not decline meetings or rearrange your week for you.

Think about what goes into a prompt. Lazur listens and looks at the screen only while you hold its shortcut. Audio and the screenshot go to AI providers to answer, and they are not stored. Content is never used to train AI models. If your meeting notes include client or patient data, follow your employer's rules first.

blocks.title: Your team still decides
blocks.text: A helper can draft the note. It cannot make your team agree to fewer meetings. Share the rule with the team before you change the calendar.
Mistakes that keep meetings growing

items: Cutting meetings without fixing the defaults. The next invite still arrives at the old length.
Declining every invite without asking for the purpose. Ask for the goal first, then decide.
Blocking focus time but leaving it open to bookings. Mark it busy and say so in your team channel.
Moving meetings into the evening. That trades one problem for the after-8 pm trend.
Calling a shorter meeting a win when the same decisions move into Slack threads.

blocks.text: Watch for the rebound. When you cut meetings, chat threads can grow to fill the space. Check your Slack activity after the first few weeks, and look for threads that replace a call. Pin a short written rule to the channel so people know when a call is still needed.
Next steps this week

Pick one change this week. A default length takes a few minutes to change, and you can undo it. Run the audit on Monday, change one default before Wednesday, then repeat the audit the following Monday. The comparison tells you more than any benchmark.

If you want help with the writing and setup on your Mac, see the [download page](/download) or the [pricing page](/pricing). Product managers who live in Slack, Notion or Linear can read these guides: [Slack for product managers](/for/product-managers/slack), [Notion for product managers](/for/product-managers/notion) and [Linear for product managers](/for/product-managers/linear).

faq.question: How many hours in meetings each week is too many?
faq.answer: No study sets one number for every role. Harvard Business Review reports that executives average nearly 23 hours a week in meetings. Use that as a reference point, then check your own week. If meetings push deep work into evenings or leave no time to write, the load is too heavy for you.

faq.question: Do meeting-free days really improve productivity?
faq.answer: The MIT Sloan study reports higher productivity with meeting-free days, including 71% with two days a week. The figures come from employee pulse surveys, so they show what people reported. The benefits level off after meetings fall 60%, so start with a steady cut.

faq.question: Can I shorten all my meetings on a Mac?
faq.answer: In Outlook for Mac, go to Outlook > Preferences > Calendar and click Configure next to Shorten duration for all events. The setting applies per email account. Google's Workspace guidance suggests a 25 minute default for meetings, but your admin may control that setting.

faq.question: Is it okay to decline a meeting my manager runs?
faq.answer: Ask for the purpose and the outcome first. Offer a written update or a shorter call if that meets the same goal. Follow your team's norms and keep your manager informed. Do not decline quietly and hope nobody notices.

faq.question: Does Focus stop meeting invites?
faq.answer: Focus lets selected people and apps through. Focus Filters change how Calendar and Mail behave while that Focus is on. Focus does not turn down invites on its own. I found no outcome data showing that Focus reduces meeting load.

faq.question: Does Lazur join meetings or decline them for me?
faq.answer: No. Lazur does not click buttons or operate other apps for you. It listens and looks at the screen only while you hold its shortcut. You can ask it to draft a decline note or add a Calendar event, then you review the result yourself.

costs.title: Less time for product thinking
costs.text: Specs, analysis and tradeoff work need long stretches. Atlassian's State of Teams 2024 survey covered 5,000 knowledge workers. It says people in poor meeting cultures spend 50% more time in unnecessary meetings than on high-priority work. Treat it as a vendor survey, not an independent audit.

costs.title: Evenings that absorb the workday
costs.text: Microsoft's June 2025 report shows meetings after 8 pm rising 16% year over year. That pattern can push deep work into the evening, when you have less energy to do it well. The research on burnout is indirect, so treat this as a reasonable worry rather than a settled finding.

costs.title: Your pay, in dollars
costs.text: The U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics reports median annual pay of $175,140 for computer and information systems managers in May 2025. That is a proxy, not a product manager figure. Use your own salary, divide it by your working hours, then apply that rate to the excess hours from your audit.

causes.title: Default meeting lengths fill the calendar
causes.text: Many calendars start every event at 30 minutes, and meetings grow to fill the slot. Google's Workspace hybrid work help suggests a 25 minute default, and ending meetings 5 to 10 minutes early. Defaults matter because nobody chooses them on purpose. They get accepted, invite after invite.

causes.title: Recurring invites outlive their purpose
causes.text: A meeting created for a launch often keeps its slot after the launch ends. Nobody wants to be the one who cancels the series. Recurring invites also hide the cost, because the series looks like one item on the calendar. Review each series once a quarter and ask whether it still needs to exist.

causes.title: Status meetings replace written updates
causes.text: Many product teams hold a meeting so people can hear the news. A written update could do the same job in less time, and people can reread it. Status calls survive because they feel safe. Written updates are easy to skip, so the call stays.

causes.title: Fear of missing a decision
causes.text: Attendees add themselves to invites as insurance. If a decision might happen, people want to be present. That habit makes every meeting bigger than it needs to be. Optional attendance and a written summary after each call reduce the fear, but only if the team trusts the summaries.

causes.title: Missing specs turn into calls
causes.text: A meeting is often a stand-in for a missing document. If the PRD is vague, people book calls to ask what you meant. Each call takes a slot from the whole group. Writing the decision down in Notion or Linear before the call removes many of these meetings.

causes.title: Global teams push meetings to the edges
causes.text: When stakeholders work in different regions, someone gets an early or late call. Microsoft's June 2025 report found meetings after 8 pm rose 16% year over year, which fits this pattern. The report does not prove the cause, so treat this as a likely contributor, not a proven one.

fixes.title: Add a purpose line to every invite
fixes.text: Start each invite with one line that names the decision or the output. If there is no decision, offer a written update instead. Attendees can then decline without guessing. This takes a minute per invite and needs no tool at all.

fixes.title: Decline with a written alternative
fixes.text: A decline works better when it offers something in return. Say what you need from the meeting, then offer a written update or a shorter call later. Lazur can draft the note, but you should read it, edit it and send it yourself.

fixes.title: Pick the weakest recurring meeting first
fixes.text: List the recurring meetings you own or attend. Start with the one that has the weakest reason to exist. Replace it with a written update for two weeks, then judge whether anyone missed the call. Most teams can answer that question quickly.

fixes.title: Use Focus to shield deep work
fixes.text: Open System Settings > Focus and set up a Focus for deep work. Allow your manager and your launch lead through with Allowed People. Add a Focus Filter for Calendar so Calendar behaves differently during that Focus. This does not reduce invites, but it cuts the pings that pull you out of focus.

fixes.title: Audit each recurring series every quarter
fixes.text: Once a quarter, list every recurring meeting on your calendar. Ask whether the series still has a purpose, who needs it, and whether a written update would do the job. Cancel or shrink the weakest ones. Log each decision in a Google Sheets tab so you can compare later.

fixes.title: Agree on a team norm in writing
fixes.text: Propose a short norm in writing. Meetings need a purpose, default lengths are shorter, and one day a week stays quiet. Small team rules work better than a company-wide ban. Ask your manager to review the norm after a month, then keep what worked.

plan.text: Set your default meeting duration in Outlook > Preferences > Calendar, or ask IT whether Google Calendar defaults can change for your team. Try the shorter length on your next two recurring syncs.

plan.text: Write a short proposal for one meeting-free day a week. Name the days that fit your launch rhythm. Block them as recurring events so people see them before they book.

plan.text: Compare your total meeting minutes and the share tagged decision with Monday's log. If the total barely moved, pick the next largest recurring meeting and repeat the plan next week.
